Effect of Microbial Necromass Deactivation 
Method on Radish Growth in Lunar 
Regolith Simulant 
Abstract: Sustained human presence on the 
Moon will require bioregenerative agricultural 
systems capable of producing food using in-situ 
resources. Lunar regolith is inherently sterile and 
lacks organic carbon, microbial nutrient cycling, 
and bioavailable nitrogen and phosphorus, 
severely constraining plant growth. One strategy 
for 
overcoming 
these 
limitations 
is 
the 
incorporation of microbial necromass, the non-
living residual biomass of microbial cells, which 
contains 
structurally 
complex 
organic 
compounds capable of acting as slow-release 
nutrient reservoirs while improving soil structure 
and water retention. In lunar habitats, microbial 
biomass would naturally accumulate in waste-
recycling systems, composting units, and other 
bioregenerative life-support bioreactors that 
process human waste and plant residues. When 
microbial communities die or are intentionally 
sterilized within these life-support systems, they 
produce necromass that could potentially be 
recycled as a soil amendment for extraterrestrial 
agriculture. 
This study investigated whether sterile microbial 
necromass can enhance plant growth in lunar 
regolith simulant and whether the microbial 
inactivation pathway alters its effectiveness as a 
soil amendment. Radish (Raphanus sativus) was 
cultivated in three regolith treatments: untreated 
regolith (control), regolith amended with heat-
killed 
microbial 
necromass, 
and 
regolith 
amended 
with 
ethanol-killed 
microbial 
necromass, with necromass incorporated at 15% 
by dry mass. 
Across replicate trials, necromass amendments 
substantially 
improved 
plant 
performance 
relative to untreated regolith over the 20-day 
growth period. On average across trials, mean 
plant height increased from 6.3 cm in the control 
treatment to 14.2 cm with heat-killed 
necromass and 14.1 cm with ethanol-killed 
necromass, representing approximately a 120% 
increase in growth. Leaf production increased 
from an average of 5 leaves in the control to 36 
leaves in the heat-treated system and 22 leaves 
in the ethanol treatment, while necromass-
amended plants maintained higher physiological 
health scores and reduced wilting. Microbial 
necromass 
significantly 
increased 
plant 
productivity, with mean fresh biomass rising 
from 0.21 g in the control to 0.68 g (ethanol-
treated) and 1.03 g (heat-treated), confirming 
enhanced 
nutrient 
availability 
in 
regolith 
systems. 
Overall, 
heat-killed 
necromass 
produced 
the 
strongest 
growth 
response, 
generating slightly greater plant height, fresh 
biomass and substantially higher leaf production 
than ethanol-killed necromass, although both 
treatments 
significantly 
improved 
plant 
performance relative to untreated regolith. These 
findings demonstrate that recycled microbial 
necromass, particularly heat-inactivated biomass, 
can function as a biologically derived soil 
amendment for lunar agriculture, supporting 
nutrient 
recycling 
and 
sustainable 
crop 
production 
within 
closed-loop 
life-support 
systems. This approach directly addresses the 
fundamental limitation of lunar regolith—its 
severe nutrient deficiency—by enabling the in-
situ conversion of waste microbial biomass into a 
functional growth resource, providing a novel 
closed-loop solution that transforms waste 
streams into usable biological inputs and 
eliminating 
dependence 
on 
Earth-supplied 
materials. Importantly, microbial biomass is 
continuously generated as a byproduct of 
bioregenerative life-support systems, making it a 
self-renewing 
resource 
stream 
that 
can 
potentially sustain long-term agricultural cycles 
in closed extraterrestrial habitats in a novel 
manner. 
Introduction: Sustained human presence on the 
Moon requires agricultural systems capable of 
producing food using in-situ resources while 
minimizing dependence on resupply from Earth. 
Lunar regolith, however, differs fundamentally 
from terrestrial soil. Formed through billions of 
years of meteoritic bombardment and physical 
weathering rather than biological processes, 
regolith 
lacks 
organic 
matter, 
microbial 
ecosystems, and biologically mediated nutrient 
cycling. Although it contains mineral elements 
such as silicon, aluminum, calcium, and iron, it is 
severely deficient in organic carbon and 
bioavailable nitrogen and phosphorus, making it 
inherently unsuitable for sustained plant growth. 
Recent experimental work has demonstrated that 
plants can germinate in authentic lunar regolith 
samples returned during the Apollo missions. 
However, plant development remains strongly 
constrained in these substrates. In a landmark 
study, Arabidopsis thaliana was successfully 
germinated in lunar regolith but exhibited 
reduced biomass accumulation, physiological 
stress, and altered gene expression associated 
with nutrient limitation and abiotic stress (Ferl & 
Paul, 2022). These findings indicate that although 
regolith can physically support germination, the 
absence of organic nutrient pools and microbial 
nutrient 
cycling 
prevents 
long-term 
plant 
productivity. Several strategies have been 
proposed 
to 
overcome 
these 
limitations, 
including the addition of terrestrial soil 
amendments, synthetic fertilizers, composted 
plant 
residues, 
or 
engineered 
microbial 
communities. 
However, 
many 
of 
these 
approaches rely on materials that would require 
continual importation from Earth or large-scale 
biological infrastructure that may be difficult to 
maintain in early extraterrestrial habitats. 
Consequently, 
current 
research 
in 
space 
agriculture increasingly emphasizes closed-loop 
resource recycling systems capable of converting 
biological waste streams into usable nutrients 
within life-support architectures. 
One potential nutrient source within closed-loop 
life-support systems is microbial necromass, the 
residual non-living biomass produced when

microbial 
cells 
die 
or 
are 
intentionally 
inactivated. In terrestrial soils, the continuous 
turnover of microbial communities generates 
necromass composed of cellular structural 
components 
including 
proteins, 
lipids, 
polysaccharides, and amino-sugar–containing 
cell wall fragments. Soil biogeochemistry studies 
show that these residues form a major fraction of 
stable soil organic matter and represent an 
important reservoir of plant-available carbon and 
nitrogen (Liang et al., 2019). Necromass 
accumulation is commonly identified through 
amino sugar biomarkers such as muramic acid 
and glucosamine, which originate from bacterial 
and fungal cell walls and persist in soil long after 
microbial death. These compounds contribute to 
the formation of relatively stable organic matter 
pools that gradually release nutrients as they 
decompose. 
In addition to acting as nutrient reservoirs, 
necromass-derived molecules can interact with 
mineral 
surfaces 
through 
organo-mineral 
associations, a process that stabilizes organic 
carbon while increasing nutrient retention and 
water-holding capacity within soils. Because 
lunar regolith is composed largely of fine mineral 
particles 
but 
lacks 
organic 
matter, 
the 
introduction of necromass could provide both a 
biochemical nutrient source and an organic 
matrix capable of improving substrate structure. 
These characteristics suggest that microbial 
necromass may function as a biologically 
generated soil amendment capable of enhancing 
the fertility of regolith-based growth substrates 
used in extraterrestrial agriculture. 
Future lunar habitats are expected to operate as 
Closed Ecological Life Support System 
(CELSS), incorporating microbial bioreactors, 
composting systems, and waste-processing units 
that recycle plant residues, food waste, and 
human waste into usable resources. Within these 
systems, microbial populations will continually 
grow and die as part of normal metabolic 
turnover, leading to the accumulation of 
substantial quantities of microbial necromass as 
an 
inevitable 
byproduct 
of 
life-support 
operations. Repurposing this necromass as a 
regolith amendment could therefore provide a 
nutrient source that is internally generated within 
the habitat rather than transported from Earth, 
making it a potentially sustainable strategy for 
extraterrestrial agriculture. Recycling microbial 
necromass in this manner aligns with the 
principle of in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), 
a key strategy in planetary exploration that seeks 
to convert locally available materials into usable 
resources for sustaining human activity beyond 
Earth. Establishing such recycling pathways 
represents the early development of artificial 
biogeochemical cycles, which are essential for 
maintaining stable nutrient flows in closed 
ecological systems. 
Despite 
extensive 
research 
on 
microbial 
necromass dynamics in terrestrial soils, its 
potential application as an amendment for 
extraterrestrial 
regolith 
remains 
largely 
unexplored. Furthermore, an important factor 
influencing necromass functionality may be the 
method by which microbial cells are inactivated 
prior to incorporation into growth substrates. In 
extraterrestrial habitats, microbial biomass will 
frequently undergo intentional sterilization to 
comply with planetary protection protocols 
designed to prevent forward contamination of 
celestial 
bodies. 
Consequently, 
microbial 
necromass produced within life-support systems 
will likely originate from sterilized microbial 
biomass rather than natural microbial death. The 
biochemical 
composition 
and 
nutrient 
availability of necromass depends on the method 
used to deactivate microbial cells. Thermal 
sterilization can denature proteins, disrupt cell 
walls, and accelerate molecular breakdown, 
potentially 
increasing 
the 
accessibility 
of 
intracellular nutrients. In contrast, ethanol 
sterilization primarily permeabilizes cellular 
membranes while preserving much of the internal 
cellular structure, which may influence the rate at 
which nutrients are released into the surrounding 
substrate. 
Therefore, this study investigates not only 
whether microbial necromass can enhance plant 
growth in lunar regolith simulant but also 
evaluates how different microbial inactivation 
pathways influence its effectiveness as a soil 
amendment. Two inactivation methods—
thermal sterilization and ethanol sterilization—
were selected because they represent sterilization 
approaches that are both technologically feasible 
within lunar habitats. Thermal sterilization could 
occur through high-temperature waste processing 
units or thermal treatment systems used to 
sanitize biological waste streams, while ethanol-
based sterilization could be implemented through 
chemical disinfection protocols routinely used to 
control microbial contamination in closed 
spacecraft environments. Both approaches align 
with sterilization procedures already used in 
spacecraft operations and could be integrated into 
life-support waste recycling systems within lunar 
habitats . 
Alternative microbial inactivation methods exist, 
including ultraviolet (UV) irradiation, autoclave-
based steam sterilization, and chemical oxidizing 
agents such as chlorine or hydrogen peroxide. 
However, these methods present limitations for 
necromass 
recycling 
in 
extraterrestrial 
agriculture. UV sterilization is primarily effective 
for surface decontamination and has limited 
penetration through dense biomass, reducing its 
effectiveness for bulk microbial substrates 
(Kowalski, 2009). Steam autoclaving requires 
substantial water resources and high-pressure 
systems, which may be impractical in early lunar 
habitats 
where 
water 
availability 
and 
infrastructure are constrained. Strong oxidizing 
chemical disinfectants such as chlorine or 
hydrogen 
peroxide 
can 
degrade 
organic 
molecules and generate reactive by-products that 
may reduce the nutritional value of microbial 
biomass intended for soil amendment (Rutala &

Weber, 2016). In contrast, thermal inactivation 
and 
ethanol 
sterilization 
can 
effectively 
deactivate 
microbial 
cells 
while 
largely 
preserving the organic molecular components 
that constitute necromass, making them suitable. 
 
Experimental Design: The experiment was 
conducted using a controlled indoor plant growth 
setup in a home environment to allow continuous 
daily monitoring under stable conditions. Plants 
were grown under natural daylight with an 
approximately 16 h light / 8 h dark photoperiod 
at an ambient temperature of ~28 °C. This 
temperature range was selected because radish 
germination and early vegetative metabolism 
occur optimally between 20–30 °C, where 
enzymatic activity, respiration rates, and cellular 
division 
processes 
supporting 
seedling 
establishment 
are 
maximized. 
Extended 
photoperiod conditions approximate controlled-
environment agriculture systems used in space 
crop 
production, 
where 
increased 
light 
availability enhances photosynthetic carbon 
assimilation and accelerates early biomass 
accumulation. 
Three substrate treatments were established: 
(1) control-100 % regolith simulant, 
(2) regolith amended with heat-killed 
microbial necromass, (3) regolith amended 
with ethanol-killed microbial necromass. 
 
Microbial necromass will be derived from a 
standardized compost tea batch and rendered 
non-viable via heat or ethanol treatment to test 
whether the mode of necromass inactivation 
influences plant growth responses. Heat-killed 
necromass will be produced via boiling, 
followed by filtration, rinsing with sterile 
distilled water, and air-drying. Ethanol-killed 
necromass will be prepared using a 70% ethanol 
treatment, with repeated rinsing to eliminate 
residual solvent prior to drying. Necromass was 
prepared using a standardized protocol from a 
single homogenized batch of compost tea to 
ensure consistency. 
 
To confirm effective microbial inactivation and 
prevent residual viable microorganisms from 
affecting plant growth, sterility of both 
necromass treatments will be assessed using a 
closed-container moisture-activated regrowth 
assay. Subsamples will be placed in clean 
transparent containers, moistened with sterile 
distilled water, and loosely sealed to allow 
limited gas exchange. Containers will be 
incubated at room temperature (22–28 °C) for 
five days and examined daily for indicators of 
microbial activity, including turbidity, gas 
production, biofilm formation, visible fungal 
growth, and odor changes. Absence of these 
indicators will indicate successful inactivation. 
A negative control with distilled water and a 
positive control with untreated compost residue 
will verify absence of contamination and 
suitability of growth conditions. Differences in 
regrowth, if observed, will contextualize 
potential effects on necromass biochemical 
integrity rather than microbial viability. 
In amended treatments, microbial necromass 
constituted 15 % of the substrate by dry mass, 
producing a mixture of 204 g regolith simulant 
and 36 g necromass per pot (240 g total). This 
proportion 
was 
selected 
to 
introduce 
a 
biologically meaningful organic carbon and 
nitrogen 
input 
while 
maintaining 
the 
mineralogical dominance of the regolith 
matrix (85 %). Preserving regolith as the 
primary structural component more realistically 
represents 
extraterrestrial 
soil 
amendment 
scenarios in which organic material availability is 
limited and recycled biological residues function 
as supplements rather than complete soil 
replacements. From a soil biogeochemistry 
perspective, this amendment level is sufficient to 
introduce 
microbial-derived 
biomolecules—
including proteins, lipids, polysaccharides, and 
cell-wall amino sugars—that can contribute to 
nutrient availability, enhance water retention, and 
promote organo-mineral interactions between 
organic molecules and regolith particles. Such 
interactions are known to stabilize organic carbon 
and improve nutrient retention in terrestrial soils, 
suggesting similar mechanisms may enhance 
substrate functionality in regolith-based systems. 
Each pot contained 240 g of substrate, a mass 
selected to provide sufficient rooting volume for 
radish seedling development while maintaining 
consistent substrate depth across treatments. 
Uniform substrate depth supports homogeneous 
water distribution and oxygen diffusion within 
the regolith matrix, reducing variability in root-
zone moisture availability. Due to the limited 
availability of regolith simulant (2 kg total 
provided), the experiment was constrained to six 
pots across three treatments, preventing the 
inclusion of additional replicates or treatment 
groups. 
Two replicate pots were prepared for each 
treatment (six pots total). Each pot was planted 
with five radish (Raphanus sativus) seeds sown 
at a uniform depth of approximately 1 cm and 
distributed evenly across the substrate surface. 
This 
sowing 
depth 
follows 
agronomic 
recommendations for small-seeded Brassicaceae 
crops, ensuring sufficient moisture contact for 
seed imbibition while minimizing mechanical 
resistance during hypocotyl emergence. The use 
of five seeds per pot provided a reliable sample 
size for germination observations while allowing 
adequate spacing within the confined substrate 
volume to reduce inter-plant competition for 
water, nutrients, and rooting space. Radish 
(Raphanus sativus) was selected as the 
experimental crop due to its rapid germination, 
short growth cycle, and high germination 
reliability, characteristics that make it widely 
used as a model organism in controlled-
environment agriculture experiments. These 
traits make radish particularly suitable for short-
duration studies designed to evaluate substrate 
fertility and early plant developmental responses. 
Plant growth was monitored over a 20-day 
cultivation period. All pots were irrigated using

distilled water at identical times and intervals to 
standardize soil moisture while preventing the 
introduction of external dissolved nutrients that 
could confound treatment effects. To further 
minimize environmental bias, pot positions were 
rotated daily, reducing potential spatial variation 
in light intensity or microclimatic gradients 
across the growth environment. 
Research question: How does the microbial 
inactivation pathway (thermal vs. chemical 
sterilization) influence the effectiveness of sterile 
microbial necromass as a soil amendment for 
supporting plant growth in simulated lunar 
regolith? 
 
Hypothesis : It is hypothesized that radish plants 
grown in lunar regolith amended with microbial 
necromass will exhibit significantly greater 
germination success, vegetative growth, and 
physiological performance than plants grown in 
untreated regolith. Lunar regolith is inherently 
devoid of organic carbon, biologically mediated 
nutrient cycling, and stable soil aggregates, 
resulting in extremely limited availability of 
plant-accessible nitrogen, poor water retention, 
and weak nutrient adsorption capacity. Microbial 
necromass represents a concentrated reservoir of 
biologically derived organic matter composed of 
structurally complex biomolecules—including 
proteins, lipids, polysaccharides, nucleic acids, 
and amino-sugar–containing microbial cell wall 
polymers such as peptidoglycan and chitin. As 
these 
compounds 
undergo 
biochemical 
decomposition and mineralization, they can 
release plant-available nitrogen and carbon while 
forming 
organo–mineral 
associations 
with 
regolith particles that enhance moisture retention, 
nutrient adsorption, and substrate aggregation, 
improving the physicochemical environment for 
root growth and rhizosphere nutrient acquisition. 
It is further hypothesized that the microbial 
inactivation pathway used to generate necromass 
will influence the biochemical accessibility and 
nutrient-release dynamics of necromass-derived 
organic 
matter. 
Heat-inactivated 
microbial 
necromass is predicted to promote greater plant 
growth 
than 
ethanol-inactivated 
necromass 
because 
thermal 
sterilization 
denatures 
intracellular proteins, disrupts lipid membranes, 
and partially degrades structural macromolecules 
within microbial cells. This structural breakdown 
is expected to increase the accessibility of 
intracellular 
compounds—including 
amino 
acids, peptides, soluble organic carbon, and 
nitrogen-containing 
metabolites—thereby 
accelerating microbial mineralization processes 
and enhancing the release of plant-available 
nutrients into the surrounding substrate. In 
contrast, 
ethanol 
sterilization 
primarily 
permeabilizes 
cellular 
membranes 
while 
preserving much of the internal cellular 
architecture 
and 
membrane-associated 
biomolecules., which may slow the release of 
nutrient-rich biomolecules during early plant 
development. Accordingly, growth is expected to 
follow the trend: heat-inactivated necromass > 
ethanol-inactivated 
necromass 
> 
untreated 
regolith, with the control limited by low nutrients 
and poor retention. These findings may provide a 
insight forrepurposing microbial biomass as a 
regenerative 
amendment 
for 
ISRU-based, 
sustainable lunar agriculture 
Variables 
Independent 
Variable(s): 
The 
independent 
variable in this investigation is the soil 
amendment condition, defined by both the 
presence of microbial necromass and the 
method used to inactivate the microbial 
biomass 
prior 
to 
incorporation. 
Three 
treatment levels were established: (1) untreated 
lunar regolith simulant (control), (2) regolith with 
heat-inactivated microbial necromass, and (3) 
regolith 
with 
ethanol-inactivated 
microbial 
necromass. This variable was deliberately 
selected because it most directly represents the 
primary limiting factor for plant growth in 
lunar regolith: the absence of organic matter 
and bioavailable nutrients. By introducing 
microbial necromass, this variable directly tests 
whether restoring a biologically derived nutrient 
pool can transform regolith from an inert 
substrate into a functionally viable plant 
growth medium, making it the most relevant and 
representative variable for evaluating plant 
growth potential in extraterrestrial systems. 
The choice of microbial necromass as the 
variable is highly innovative and strategically 
optimal compared to alternatives such as 
synthetic fertilizers, imported soil, or engineered 
microbial inoculants. Synthetic fertilizers require 
transport from Earth, and engineered or terrestrial 
alternatives need complex maintenance or are 
impractical for large scale transport, whereas 
microbial necromass is a continuously generated, 
renewable byproduct of closed-loop waste 
processing, requiring no additional importation. 
Furthermore, microbial necromass inherently 
contains all major biochemical components 
required for plant growth directly addressing 
the key deficiencies of lunar regolith. This makes 
it not only the most feasible solution under lunar 
resource constraints, but also makes it t 
biologically complete and efficient. 
The inclusion of two distinct inactivation 
pathways (thermal vs. chemical sterilization) 
further elevates the variable by introducing a 
mechanistic 
and 
application-oriented 
dimension. These pathways are realistic within 
lunar habitats and influence the structural 
integrity of microbial cells, thereby affecting the 
rate and accessibility of nutrient release. This 
allows the experiment to evaluate which 
processing method maximizes effectiveness, 
informing how waste-processing systems should 
be designed. This variable was prioritized over all 
other possible variables because it uniquely 
integrates plant biology, waste recycling, 
system sustainability, and habitat feasibility

into a single testable factor. It represents the 
highest-impact intervention for improving 
plant growth in regolith, while also addressing 
engineering constraints. As a result, it forms the 
basis of a highly original experiment that goes 
beyond 
measuring 
growth 
outcomes 
to 
evaluating a novel practical, closed-loop 
agricultural solution for the Moon. 
Dependent Variable(s): The dependent variables 
were selected to provide a comprehensive, 
multi-dimensional assessment of plant growth, 
physiological performance, and substrate 
functionality, 
directly 
reflecting 
the 
effectiveness of microbial necromass as a soil 
amendment under lunar conditions. Each variable 
was chosen based on its ability to represent a 
critical component of plant productivity in 
nutrient-limited 
environments, 
ensuring 
alignment with the research question and 
hypothesis. 
Final fresh biomass, measured after 20 days, was 
the primary dependent variable as it provides the 
most integrated measure of plant performance, 
reflecting cumulative nutrient uptake, water 
retention, and physiological health, and directly 
representing resource-use efficiency in lunar 
agriculture. Biomass directly represents the 
ultimate objective of lunar agriculture—
maximizing food production efficiency per 
unit resource, making it the most meaningful 
indicator. Compared to other potential primary 
measures such as plant height or leaf count, 
biomass captures total carbon assimilation and 
resource conversion, providing a more complete 
representation of overall performance. 
Secondary dependent variables were selected 
to capture specific growth processes and identify 
mechanistic differences between treatments 
that may not be fully reflected in biomass alone. 
Germination percentage was measured to assess 
early-stage substrate suitability and the ability of 
necromass amendments to support seed viability 
under regolith conditions. Mean plant height and 
leaf count were recorded as indicators of 
vegetative growth and photosynthetic capacity, 
reflecting 
how 
effectively 
plants 
convert 
available resources into above-ground biomass. 
Additionally, visual plant health was assessed 
using a standardized 1–5 scoring system based on 
wilting, discoloration, and structural integrity. 
This variable captures physiological stress 
responses that may not be immediately reflected 
in quantitative growth measurements, providing 
a rapid and sensitive indicator of plant condition. 
Together, these variables were deliberately 
selected because they allow for a layered 
evaluation of plant growth. This approach 
increases experimental sensitivity and ensures 
that both quantitative productivity outcomes 
and underlying biological processes are 
captured. This provides a more reliable and 
nuanced 
understanding 
of 
how 
microbial 
necromass—and its method of inactivation—
affects plant growth. 
Controlled Variables: To ensure that observed 
differences were solely due to the independent 
variable, all other growth conditions were 
standardized based on their known influence on 
plant development. Plant species (Raphanus 
sativus) was kept constant to eliminate genetic 
variability.. Using multiple species could 
increase generalizability but would introduce 
confounding variation. Lunar regolith simulant 
was identical across treatments to maintain 
consistent mineral composition and baseline 
nutrient availability. Using terrestrial soil would 
introduce organic matter and microbial activity, 
masking the specific effects of necromass. 
Necromass concentration (15% by mass) was 
held constant to isolate the effect of inactivation 
pathway rather than amendment quantity. Testing 
multiple concentrations would introduce an 
additional variable and reduce clarity. The 
selected level represents a realistic and effective 
amendment proportion. Pot size and substrate 
mass (240 g) were standardized to maintain 
consistent rooting volume, aeration, and moisture 
distribution. Seed number and planting depth 
were controlled by planting five seeds per pot at 
~1 cm depth, ensuring uniform germination 
conditions while minimizing competition and 
emergence variability. Lighting conditions (~16 
h natural daylight) were kept consistent to 
ensure equal photosynthetic input. Artificial 
systems could offer tighter control, but natural 
light provided a practical and sufficiently stable 
approximation 
of 
extended 
photoperiod 
conditions. Water volume, timing, and type 
(distilled water) were standardized to eliminate 
variation in hydration and nutrient input. 
Distilled water was used specifically to avoid 
introducing 
external 
dissolved 
minerals. 
Environmental conditions (indoor, ~28 °C) 
were maintained to minimize fluctuations in 
temperature and humidity. Outdoor conditions 
were avoided due to uncontrolled variability. 
Apparatus and Materials 
Biological Materials: Lunar regolith simulant 
(~1.3 kg total used), Leaf compost (500 g) , 
Radish seeds (Raphanus sativus, ≥30 seeds), 
Distilled water (≥4 L) 
Containers and Labware: 6 planting pots (400 
mL, with drainage), 6 collection trays , 3 mixing 
containers (≥1 L), Heat-resistant container (≥1 
L), 6 transparent containers (100 mL) for 
sterility test, Filter cloth + mesh, Drying trays 
Measurement Equipment: Digital balance 
(±0.1 g), Measuring cylinders (100 mL, 500 
mL), Ruler (mm scale), Thermometer 
Reagents: 70% ethanol (250 mL used) 
Procedure 
Phase 1: Microbial Necromass Preparation 
 
a) Compost Tea Preparation 
1. Add 550 g leaf compost to a container. 
2. Add 3.0 L distilled water (1:6 ratio). 
3. Stir thoroughly and cover loosely. 
4. Steep for 18 hours at 25–28 °C, stirring 
periodically.

b) Biomass Extraction and Washing 
5. Filter mixture through mesh + cloth. 
6. Collect ~400 g wet biomass. 
7. Add 200 mL distilled water, stir, and refilter. 
8. Repeat washing 3 times. 
9. Divide biomass into two equal portions (~180 
g each). 
c)Heat-Inactivation 
10. Submerge Portion A in 250 mL distilled 
water. 
11. Boil at 100 °C for 25 minutes. 
12.Cool, filter, and rinse with ~400 mL distilled 
water (3–4 rinses). 
13. Air-dry 24–48 hours to ~80 g dry mass. 
d) Ethanol Inactivation 
14.Submerge Portion B in 250 mL of 70% 
ethanol. 
15. Soak for 30 minutes, stirring periodically. 
16. Filter and rinse with ~500 mL distilled 
water (4–5 rinses). 
17. Air-dry 24–48 hours to ~80 g dry mass. 
Phase 2: Sterility Verification 
f)Setup 
18. Place 1.5 g of each treated necromass into 
containers. Hence 2 containers total (1 each) 
19. Add 10 mL distilled water to each. 
20. Prepare controls: Positive -> 1.5 g 
untreated compost + 10 mL water 
Negative -> 10 mL distilled water only 
g)Incubation and Observation 
21. Incubate at 25 °C (22–28 °C range) for 5 
days. 
22. Observe daily for turbidity, gas, odor, or 
fungal growth 
23. Proceed only if no microbial activity is 
observed in treated samples. 
 
Phase 3: Growth Medium Preparations 
h) Substrate Composition (per pot = 240 g) 
24. Control (2 pots): 240 g regolith each Total 
used: 480 g regolith 
25. Heat Treatment (2 pots): 204 g regolith + 
36 g necromass each Total used: 408 g regolith 
+ 72 g necromass 
26. Ethanol Treatment (2 pots): 204 g regolith 
+ 36 g necromass each Total used: 408 g 
regolith + 72 g necromass 
27) Totals Across: Total regolith used: 480 + 
408 + 408 = 1296 g (~1.30 kg), Total 
necromass used: 72 + 72 = 144 g 
i) Mixing and Moistening 
28) Mix each treatment separately. 
29) Add 50 mL distilled water per pot (240 g 
substrate).Allow to equilibrate 30 minutes. 
Phase 4: Pot Setup and Planting 
30. Add 240 g substrate to each pot. Prepare 6 
pots total (2 per treatment) 
31. Rinse seeds with water (~50 mL each). 
32) Plant 5 seeds per pot at 1.0 cm depth. 
33) Space evenly and cover lightly (~0.5 cm). 
34) Add 20 mL distilled water per pot. 
35) Record initial mass of each pot. 
Phase 5: Growth 
36)Maintain: Light: 14–16 h/day Temperature: 
26–28 °C. Randomize/rotate pots every 2 days. 
37.Add 15 mL distilled water per pot every ~2 
days (or when dry). 
38. Record every 2 days: Germination (% , 
Plant height (cm), Leaf count, Health (1–5) 
39.After 20 days, Remove plants carefully. 
40.Wash roots (~50 mL distilled water per 
sample). Measure root length (mm). 
41. Blot dry for 30 seconds. Measure fresh 
biomass (g). Calculate mean and standard 
deviation 
Qualitative Analysis: 
• Control plants (C1, C2): 
• 
Early stage (Day 5–7): leaves appeared light 
green but already less vibrant than treated groups 
• 
Mid 
stage 
(Day 
7–11): 
clear 
yellowing 
(chlorosis) developed, especially in older leaves 
• 
Visible leaf curling, drooping, and loss of 
rigidity became prominent 
• 
Late stage (Day 14–20): leaves turned brown, 
dry, and brittle, with complete collapse of 
structure and immense wilting 
• 
Final observation: plants appeared desiccated 
and dead, with no visible turgor or green 
pigmentation except for 1 stem 
• Heat-treated necromass (H1, H2):

Wilting and curling indicate loss of turgor

A) Integrated Growth Dynamics, System 
Divergence, and Multi-Variable Hierarchy 
Across all measured parameters (plant height, leaf 
count, health score, germination success), the 
system exhibits a non-linear, treatment-dependent 
divergence 
that 
becomes 
statistically 
and 
biologically significant from Day 5 onward (p < 
0.05). All treatments begin at 0 cm on Day 1, 
confirming a uniform germination baseline and 
minimizing seed-level variability. From Days 1–6, 
growth is dominated by seed reserve utilization and 
early substrate interaction. Heat-treated systems 
show the highest mean plant height (≈ 9.6 cm), 
consistent with enhanced nutrient accessibility 
likely driven by thermally induced structural 
breakdown of necromass. Ethanol-treated systems 
show moderate but more variable growth (≈ 6.5 
cm), indicating delayed and uneven activation of 
decomposition-mediated nutrient release. Control 
systems remain lowest (≈ 5.8 cm), reflecting 
nutrient absence and reliance on diminishing 
internal reserves. Leaf and health metrics reinforce 
early divergence: heat-treated plants maintain high 
leaf 
integrity 
(~20 
leaves) 
and 
maximal 
physiological stability, ethanol-treated systems 
show moderate but variable leaf formation (6–12 
leaves) with fluctuating health, while controls 
exhibit initial increases in leaf number and height 
driven by residual internal reserves (average of 4.5 
to 15.5 cm growth in day 4-6), while alongside 
facing declining leaf health as these resources 
become depleted (5 to 4 mean leaf health score in 
day 4-6). These trends indicate early separation of 
physiological stability despite relatively small 
absolute height differences. Replicate variability 
further differentiates treatment effects. Ethanol 
shows the widest dispersion in both height (4.6–
8.5cm) and leaf count (6–12), suggesting 
heterogeneous 
substrate 
interaction 
and 
inconsistent nutrient release dynamics. Heat-
treated systems are tightly clustered (height ~9.5–
9.7cm), indicating stable and uniform growth 
conditions, while controls show intermediate 
variability driven by stochastic depletion of seed 
reserves under nutrient limitation. Overall, the data 
supports 
a 
clear 
early-stage 
hierarchy 
(heat>ethanol>control). The rapid increase in 
height between Days 4–6 across all treatments 
reflects a typical transition from reserve-dependent 
growth to active nutrient uptake, where hypocotyl 
elongation and early leaf expansion produce a short 
phase 
of 
accelerated 
vertical 
growth

B) Early Overtaking Events and Kinetic 
Reversal Mechanisms (Days 6–8) A critical 
system-level overtaking occurs between Days 5–7, 
where ethanol-treated plants surpass heat-treated 
plants in height (ethanol ≈ 10.75 cm vs heat ≈ 8.7 
cm mean). This reversal while could be anomalous, 
however it is observed over both trials, has a high 
chance of biologically grounded in decomposition 
kinetics: ethanol treatment initially suppresses 
microbial 
efficiency 
but 
later 
enhances 
solubilization of organic compounds, producing a 
delayed inital nutrient surge. This is reflected 
across variables: ethanol leaf count increases (10–
12 range), indicating synchronized biomass 
expansion. On the other hand, the apparent 
reduction in plant height observed in control (5.80 
to 5.65) and heat-treated (9.6 to 8.7) systems after 
Day 6 does not represent true negative growth, but 
is instead attributable to a transient loss of turgor 
pressure and stem bending under emerging 
physiological stress, potentially driven by short-
term water limitation or uneven water distribution 
within the substrate. As plant height was measured 
vertically from the soil surface to the highest point, 
partial wilting or curvature of the stem can produce 
lower recorded values despite continued biomass 
presence. Importantly, this does not preclude 
subsequent recovery, as restoration of water 
balance can re-establish turgidity and upright 
growth, allowing height to increase again in later 
time points. This interpretation is supported by 
concurrent declines in leaf health scores and the 
onset of wilting, indicating that structural 
measurements become temporarily decoupled from 
physiological status during early stress conditions. 
 In parallel, leaf count declines from higher early 
values (up to 18 leaves at Day 5) to lower values by 
Day 7 (16–12), showing that biomass loss begins 
while height remains relatively stable, establishing 
the first clear decoupling between structural growth 
and functional stability. Health scores also decline 
from near-optimal or moderate levels at Day 5 (5, 
3) to reduced values by Day 7 (3, 3), reflecting 
early 
physiological 
stress 
and 
chlorophyll 
degradation. Wilting is already present from Day 6 
(“Yes”), confirming that water transport disruption 
precedes visible structural collapse. Collectively, 
these trends demonstrate early multi-variable 
decoupling in control systems, where height no 
longer reliably reflects physiological condition due 
to nitrogen limitation and impaired water balance. 
This differential response is likely due to the 
initially rapid growth surge in heat-treated systems, 
which leads to temporary depletion of readily 
available 
nutrient 
fractions 
and 
short-term 
physiological adjustment, along with complete 
nutrient limitation in controls, both exacerbating 
early water stress, whereas ethanol-treated systems 
benefit from delayed nutrient release, sustaining 
turgor maintenance and continued structural 
expansion during this phase; however, if residual or 
delayed-release nutrient pools remain available, 
subsequent recovery and renewed growth are still 
possible. 
 
C) 
Mid-Growth 
Stabilization, 
Divergent 
Resource Pathways, and Functional Tradeoffs 
(Days 8–12) Between Days 8–12, ethanol-treated 
plants exhibit the highest mid-phase growth rate, 
with mean height increasing from 10.75 to 13.65 
cm alongside continued leaf production (11 to 16 
leaves). This follows an earlier middle phase of 
rapid growth (Days 4–6), indicating that the system 
has transitioned from an initial middle surge to a 
more moderated but sustained growth phase, likely 
due to partial depletion of readily accessible 
delayed nutrient fractions. This pattern remains 
consistent 
with 
gradual 
solubilization 
and 
continued breakdown of compounds within the 
ethanol-treated necromass, maintaining nutrient 
availability during the mid-growth phase. In 
contrast, heat-treated plants show a moderate 
increase in height (8.7 to ~11.3 cm) with minimal 
change in leaf number, representing recovery from 
the earlier transient decline and indicating 
stabilization of resource availability. This suggests 
that heat-treated systems experienced an initial 
rapid growth phase driven by early nutrient 
availability, followed by a temporary decline due to 
depletion of readily accessible nutrients and short-
term physiological adjustment, and a subsequent 
recovery as delayed-release nutrient fractions 
became available, allowing growth to increase 
again. Overall, these results demonstrate that 
microbial inactivation method governs the timing 
of nutrient availability, producing a mid-phase 
growth peak in ethanol-treated systems and a more 
stabilized growth profile in heat-treated systems. 
4. System Failure Thresholds and Collapse 
Consolidation 
in 
Controls 
(Days 
8–14) 
During Days 9–14, control plants exhibited 
synchronized 
collapse 
across 
all 
measured 
variables, including rapid leaf loss (14-> 7), sharp 
declines in health scores (3 ->1.5), and persistent 
wilting. This indicates a transition from growth-
dominated metabolism to survival metabolism, 
where respiratory demand exceeds photosynthetic 
capacity due to nutrient exhaustion and progressive 
chlorophyll degradation. Wilting became persistent 
rather than intermittent, reflecting loss of turgor 
pressure regulation and reduced water transport 
efficiency, likely associated with declining root 
function and osmotic imbalance. This collapse is 
consistent with compounded nitrogen limitation 
and reduced chlorophyll synthesis, leading to 
impaired 
energy 
production 
and 
eventual 
physiological failure. Despite this overall decline, 
the mean plant height shows a slight increase (4.65 
to 5.5), driven by asymmetrical survival between 
replicates, where one trial undergoes near-complete 
failure while another maintains a single dominant 
stem that continues elongation by reallocating 
limited internal resources, highlighting competitive 
resource prioritization under extreme stress 
conditions. 
5. Day 12-14 in Heat Killed and Ethanol: 
Surprising 
reduction 
The slight decrease in mean plant height observed 
in both heat-(11.3-11 cm height) and ethanol-
treated systems (13.65-12.9 cm height) between 
Days 12–14 does not represent true growth 
reduction but instead reflects transient wilting due 
to reduced turgor pressure, leading to minor stem 
curvature and lower recorded vertical height. This 
follows an earlier phase of rapid growth, during 
which high nutrient uptake likely depleted readily 
accessible resource pools, creating a temporary 
limitation as the system adjusts to reduced 
availability, which may reflect earlier depletion of 
readily available nutrients in heat-treated systems 
and a transient physiological adjustment following 
sustained nutrient uptake in ethanol-treated

systems. The absence of increase in leaf number 
confirms minimal net biomass production during 
this interval, while leaf health remains stable in 
heat-treated systems (≈5) and only slightly declines 
in ethanol-treated systems (≈5 to ~4–4.5), 
indicating mild, non-critical stress rather than 
systemic failure. Biologically, this phase represents 
a transition between nutrient pools, where initial 
labile resources are exhausted and plants rely on 
slower-release 
or 
less 
accessible 
fractions, 
temporarily 
reducing 
growth 
efficiency. 
In 
contrast, control systems continue to show a slight 
increase in mean height due to the persistence of a 
single elongating stem, as previously described. 
Growth resumes after this phase as delayed-access 
nutrients become available and water balance is 
restored, explaining the subsequent increase in 
plant height. 
6. Late-Stage Reversal, Secondary Nutrient Pulse, 
and Dominance Shift (Days 14–20) From Days 14–
20, a second major shift in growth hierarchy occurs, 
with 
heat-treated 
systems 
re-establishing 
dominance in both height and leaf production by 
Day 20 (heat ≈ 15.4 cm vs ethanol ≈ 14.3 cm). This 
follows a previously observed mid-phase period of 
ethanol dominance, indicating a time-dependent 
reversal in treatment efficiency. During the late 
phase, heat-treated plants show a marked 
acceleration in both height gain and leaf expansion 
(≈ 20 → 38–39 leaves), suggesting renewed 
vegetative 
development 
after 
an 
earlier 
stabilization period. This pattern is consistent with 
continued structural breakdown of necromass 
under heat treatment, which likely disrupts more 
rigid cell wall components (e.g., cellulose–
hemicellulose matrices), increasing long-term 
accessibility of bound organic compounds and 
supporting sustained nutrient release in later stages. 
In contrast, ethanol-treated plants begin to stagnate 
during this phase, with growth rate slowing(12.9 to 
14.35) and leaf production continuing at a reduced 
rate (16-20), indicating reduced access to available 
nutrients and a shift toward maintenance-level 
metabolism rather than active expansion. This may 
reflect ethanol-induced disruption of membrane 
lipids and partial solubilization of easily accessible 
cytoplasmic compounds in the necromass, which 
accelerates nutrient release in the middle phase but 
leaves 
more 
structural 
polysaccharide-rich 
components less effectively broken down, leading 
to earlier depletion of readily available nutrient 
pools and reduced late-stage availability. Control 
plants remain in severe physiological decline with 
no meaningful recovery, confirming irreversible 
system failure once metabolic thresholds are 
exceeded 
under 
nutrient-limited 
conditions; 
however, a seed continues limited growth due to 
inherent 
variability 
in 
seed 
reserve 
size, 
germination 
vigor, 
and 
root 
establishment 
efficiency, 
allowing 
isolated 
individuals 
to 
temporarily persist despite overall system collapse. 
This is seen by the fact that control 1 goes to 7.7cm 
while 
control 
2 
is 
at 
4cm. 
 
Hence, this also shows that microbial necromass 
not only enhances visible growth parameters such 
as height and leaf count but also significantly 
increases total biomass production, with mean 
fresh biomass rising from 0.21 g in the control to 
0.68 g in ethanol-treated systems and 1.03 g in heat-
treated systems, confirming improved overall 
resource utilization and plant productivity in 
regolith systems. Furthermore, the greater biomass 
accumulation in heat-treated systems (1.03 g) 
compared to ethanol-treated systems (0.68 g) 
reinforces that the method of microbial inactivation 
directly influences nutrient availability, with 
thermal processing enabling more sustained and 
efficient nutrient release compared to ethanol 
treatment. The standard deviation observed across 
replicate 
trials 
reflects 
inherent 
biological 
variability within plant growth systems. Even 
under controlled conditions, individual plants may 
exhibit differences in germination timing, nutrient 
uptake efficiency, and metabolic activity, leading 
to variation in measured parameters. Therefore, the 
presence of variability does not undermine the 
reliability of the results but instead indicates the 
natural 
stochasticity 
of 
biological 
systems, 
reinforcing the importance of using mean values 
for 
accurate 
interpretation. 
 
Conclusion: This study set out to test the 
hypothesis that microbial necromass can enhance 
plant growth in lunar regolith simulant, and that the 
microbial inactivation pathway used to generate 
that necromass (thermal vs. ethanol sterilization) 
would significantly influence its effectiveness as a 
soil amendment. Overall, the results strongly 
support this hypothesis. Both necromass treatments 
substantially 
improved 
germination 
success, 
germination 
stability, 
vegetative 
growth, 
physiological health, and biomass accumulation 
relative to untreated regolith, confirming that 
recycled 
microbial 
biomass 
can 
partially 
compensate for the absence of organic matter and 
biologically mediated nutrient cycling in lunar 
regolith systems. Importantly, the consistent 
performance hierarchy (heat-treated > ethanol-
treated > control) across multiple independent 
growth metrics supports the second part of the 
hypothesis, demonstrating that both the presence of 
necromass and its processing pathway are key 
determinants of plant performance. 
However, while the hypothesis correctly predicted 
that heat-inactivated necromass would outperform 
ethanol-inactivated necromass due to increased 
structural breakdown and enhanced nutrient 
accessibility, it did not explicitly predict the time-
dependent nature of this divergence. The 
observed phase shifts in growth dynamics indicate 
that the effect of microbial inactivation is not 
constant over time but instead varies across 
developmental stages. The findings hence refine 
the original hypothesis by showing that treatment-
dependent differences arise from three distinct 
kinetic regimes governed by nutrient release 
timing, 
metabolic 
efficiency, 
and 
substrate 
accessibility. Heat-inactivated necromass promotes 
a bimodal growth trajectory, with an initial rapid 
phase driven by immediate nutrient release 
followed by a secondary acceleration sustained by 
continued decomposition of more recalcitrant 
structural components. This reflects greater 
structural disruption of microbial cells, increased 
exposure of bound organic fractions, and 
breakdown of rigid cell wall matrices (e.g., 
cellulose–hemicellulose), collectively enhancing 
long-term accessibility of organic carbon and 
nitrogen. 
In 
contrast, 
ethanol-inactivated 
necromass 
preserves 
more 
intact 
cellular 
architecture, producing a smoother, diffusion-
driven growth pattern characterized by sustained 
mid-phase 
acceleration 
due 
to 
gradual 
solubilization of organic compounds, but earlier

plateauing as readily accessible nutrient fractions 
become depleted, resulting in faster mid-stage 
availability but reduced long-term persistence. 
Control systems exhibit a progressive decline in 
growth rate, transitioning from early reserve-
dependent growth to stagnation and eventual 
regression due to the absence of exogenous nutrient 
input, confirming irreversible system failure once 
metabolic thresholds are exceeded under nutrient-
limited conditions, despite minor variability arising 
from inherent differences in seed reserve size, 
germination vigor, and early root establishment. 
Across all treatments, overtaking events, transient 
fluctuations, and rate shifts are consistent with 
decomposition-mediated nutrient dynamics rather 
than experimental error, with residual variability 
reflecting expected differences in uptake efficiency 
and microenvironmental conditions. 
Several 
key 
assumptions 
underpin 
these 
interpretations. First, it was assumed that microbial 
inactivation was complete in both treatments; 
however, while sterility was assessed using a 
regrowth-based assay, this method only detects 
culturable or actively resuscitating organisms and 
may not capture non-culturable but metabolically 
dormant survivors or resilient microbial fragments. 
A more rigorous approach would include 
molecular-level confirmation of sterilization using 
DNA-based methods such as qPCR targeting 
universal 16S/18S rRNA gene sequences or ATP 
bioluminescence assays to quantify residual 
metabolic activity, providing higher sensitivity and 
reducing 
uncertainty 
regarding 
incomplete 
microbial inactivation. Second, it was assumed that 
compost-derived necromass was compositionally 
uniform prior to treatment, despite potential 
variability in microbial community composition 
and biomass structure. Third, the study assumes 
that differences in plant performance arise 
primarily 
from 
biochemical 
differences 
in 
necromass processing rather than unmeasured 
physical differences in substrate structure (e.g., 
porosity, aggregation, bulk density, and water 
distribution), which may also have been subtly 
altered by heat or ethanol exposure. Finally, the 
interpretation assumes that regolith simulant 
adequately approximates key physicochemical 
constraints of lunar regolith, despite the absence of 
extraterrestrial conditions such as reduced gravity, 
radiation exposure, and extreme thermal cycling. 
A key limitation of this investigation is the lack of 
direct characterization of the regolith–necromass 
system, 
as 
nutrient 
availability 
(including 
bioavailable nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic 
carbon) and soil physical properties such as 
porosity and water retention were not measured. 
This limits the ability to determine whether the 
observed improvements in plant growth were 
driven primarily by increased nutrient supply or 
structural 
enhancements 
to 
the 
substrate. 
Furthermore, the composition of the necromass 
itself was not analyzed, restricting insight into how 
different inactivation methods may have influenced 
nutrient release dynamics. Future work should 
incorporate quantitative chemical and physical 
analyses of the substrate, alongside detailed 
characterization of necromass, to better resolve the 
mechanisms underlying growth enhancement. 
Experimental uncertainty may also arise from 
measurement 
limitations, 
including 
minor 
inaccuracies in height measurement, biomass 
determination, and consistency of necromass 
mixing within the regolith. While efforts were 
made to standardize procedures, small human and 
instrumental errors are inevitable. Nevertheless, 
consistent methodology across treatments ensures 
that comparisons between groups remain valid. 
 
Future experimental improvements should also 
focus on environmental standardization and 
scaling. A controlled greenhouse or growth 
chamber setup would allow precise regulation of 
temperature, humidity, CO₂ concentration, and 
light intensity, reducing environmental noise and 
enabling stronger attribution of effects to substrate 
composition alone. Increasing replication (more 
pots per treatment and independent experimental 
runs) would improve statistical power and allow 
more robust detection of subtle treatment 
differences. In addition, future studies should 
incorporate a gradient of necromass concentrations 
rather than a single fixed 15% inclusion rate, 
enabling 
determination 
of 
dose–response 
relationships 
and 
identification 
of 
optimal 
amendment levels for plant productivity in regolith 
systems. Further improvements could include 
direct biochemical characterization of necromass 
before and after inactivation (e.g., soluble nitrogen, 
carbon fractions, lipid and amino sugar content, 
amino 
sugars, 
lipid 
fractions, 
and 
carbon 
speciation), as well as measurements of substrate 
physical changes such as water retention curves, 
bulk density, porosity, and pore structure. These 
would help separate chemical nutrient effects from 
physical soil modification effects, which are likely 
both contributing to plant performance. Isotopic 
tracing (e.g., ¹⁵N-labelled biomass) would also 
allow direct confirmation that necromass-derived 
nutrients are being assimilated into plant tissues 
rather than indirectly altering substrate conditions, 
while simultaneously separating uptake efficiency 
from substrate-mediated effects. 
These results establish microbial necromass as a 
practical, 
scalable 
biological 
resource 
for 
autonomous 
agriculture 
in 
extraterrestrial 
environments, where waste is not discarded but 
engineered into a functional nutrient system. The 
demonstrated control of plant growth through 
thermally 
and 
ethanol-mediated 
deactivation 
pathways shows that nutrient release can be 
predictably tuned using processes already feasible 
under lunar-relevant conditions. Unlike current 
lunar agriculture concepts that rely on pre-
processed Earth-supplied nutrients or externally 
manufactured 
growth 
media, 
this 
work 
demonstrates 
that 
equivalent 
or 
superior 
productivity can be achieved through in-situ 
conversion of biological waste into controllable 
nutrient systems, shifting from resource import 
dependence 
to 
self-sustaining 
ecological 
production on the Moon. This strengthens the 
feasibility of sustained lunar life by enabling 
continuous food production through recycling 
biological waste into usable nutrients. Microbial 
systems can be regenerated on the Moon, and 
deactivation methods repeatedly applied, making 
this a non-finite regenerative loop unlike Earth-
dependent supply chains. Thus, waste organisms 
that would otherwise be discarded can be converted 
into food-producing inputs, showing waste can 
become food in a sustained lunar system. Within 
this framework, heat-treated necromass is the most 
effective pathway, showing higher productivity and 
greater stability than ethanol treatment while 
remaining 
feasible 
under 
lunar 
condition
